description: We are four engineers who share one question: how do you pick a safe place to land on the Moon when the Sun and Earth barely rise above the horizon? For NASA Space Apps 2026 we took on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We built a tool that ranks lunar south pole landing sites for a chosen date by sunlight, Earth visibility and terrain slope. It also shows how the ranking changes if the landing slips by two weeks.
summary: At the lunar south pole the Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so whether a lander has power and a radio link depends on the exact landing date, not only on the place. Lunar Landing Navigator is a planning tool that starts from the date: choose a landing date, time and mission length, and it ranks the 13 Artemis III candidate regions on sunlight, Earth contact and flatness for that mission, using NASA LRO terrain data. It also shows how each result changes if the landing slips, so planners can choose a site that survives a schedule change.
details:
Guided tour (start here): https://quentinliu-a11y.github.io/Lunar_Landing_Optimal_System/

Full analysis app: https://lunar-landing-navigator-team-of-aeers.streamlit.app/

Source code: https://github.com/quentinliu-a11y/Lunar_Landing_Optimal_System

WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Navigator answers one question for lunar south-pole missions: if we land on this date, which sites have sunlight and a link to Earth, and what happens if the date slips?

The user picks a landing date and time (2027–2030, UTC), the length of the surface mission (1–60 days) and the lander. A map of the south pole then shows the 13 Artemis III candidate regions, ranked for that mission. For each site the tool reports the share of the mission with the Sun above the terrain, the share with Earth above the terrain, the slope, the time until sunset and Earthset, the longest dark period and longest loss of contact, any lunar eclipse, the worst case if the landing slips by up to 14 days, and the nearest landing date that works when a site fails. Users can also enter their own coordinates.

There are two ways in, built on the same results: a guided tour for non-specialists that flies from Earth to the south pole and ends standing at the chosen site in 3D, and a full analysis app with every chart and setting, including a sky panorama, date heat maps and a CSV download.

HOW IT WORKS

For each site we computed the terrain skyline in 360 directions from NASA LOLA elevation models (40 m per pixel within 25 km, 120 m per pixel out to 300 km), for a mast 2 m above the surface. Sun and Earth directions are computed for every hour of 2027–2030 with the ERFA library and the IAU lunar rotation model. A body counts as visible when the top edge of its disc is above the skyline. Everything is computed once and stored in a lookup table, so changing the date is instant.

Sites must first pass hard limits that describe the lander (defaults: at least 95% sunlight and 95% Earth contact during the mission, mean slope at most 10°, and at least 50% long-term sunlight and Earth visibility). Passing sites are ranked by a score with dynamic weights: each factor scores its margin above the lander's limit, and the sunlight and Earth weights are reduced where that value would not survive a schedule slip. Every limit and weight can be changed.

Accuracy: our Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons (DE441) within 0.003° in elevation and 0.008° in azimuth at 10 reference points. Each site's skyline is calibrated so that its 18.6-year average sunlight equals NASA's published LOLA value. The repository contains 21 automated checks, and the guided tour matches the calculation engine in 432 tested cases.

BENEFITS

- Planners compare 13 sites for a real mission window in seconds, instead of working through existing tools one case at a time.

- The tool shows the margin, not only the answer: how much sunlight and contact are left if the launch slips.

- When a site fails, it gives the nearest dates on which the site works.

- Non-specialists get plain-language verdicts for power, radio contact, ground slope and schedule risk, and can watch the Sun set behind the real terrain in 3D.

- It also shows the Earth side of the link: which NASA Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) can see the Moon hour by hour.

INTENDED IMPACT

Long-term average maps hide large date-to-date changes. Example from the tool: Nobile Rim 1 has 100% sunlight and 100% Earth contact for a 14-day mission landing on 1 January 2028, but if that landing slips by up to 14 days the worst case is 41% sunlight and 46% Earth contact. On that date only 2 of the 13 sites meet the default limits. We want science and engineering teams to choose a site that survives a schedule change, and we want students and the public to understand why a small change of place or date matters so much at the south pole. The code and data are public, so the results can be repeated and extended to other sites.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Python (NumPy, pandas, pyerfa, Streamlit, Plotly) for the calculation engine and the analysis app. HTML, CSS, JavaScript and three.js for the guided tour and the 3D view. GitHub Pages and Streamlit Community Cloud for hosting. No special hardware. AI tools (Claude and OpenAI Codex) were used to write code and documents under the team's direction; details are in the AI section.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It starts from the date, not the place: site choice is treated as a function f(date, site, others), and that formula is the heading that fills in as the user moves through the tour.

- Stability is a ranking factor: a site that is perfect today but fragile to a schedule slip is ranked lower.

- One continuous journey: Earth at night, the launch pad, the south pole with ranked sites, then the lander's own view, with real star positions and airless lighting.

- A precomputed lookup table keeps every date change and animation smooth.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- The three main factors: sunlight (power), Earth contact (communication) and flatness (landing safety).

- Schedule slip, lunar eclipses, and the difference between long-term averages and a specific mission window.

- The lander's design: limits are settings, with presets for a Nova-C class lander (10° slope) and a crewed lander (8°).

- Honest limits: results are estimates anchored to NASA's long-term data, not mission-grade predictions. Eclipse hours are reported but not subtracted. "Earth visible" does not guarantee a link to a particular ground station. Custom coordinates use a coarser (500 m), uncalibrated terrain grid. The default 95% limits are the team's stand-ins, not NASA requirements.

TEAM

Team_of_AEers: Qiming (system architecture and optimisation), Surani (solar power and comms), Ratnesh and Zhehao (computing resources; finding data and resources).
